title: Why Two British Men Admitted Making Crop Circles in 1991 | Curiosity Case Files｜ CC字幕
description:
In September 1991, two British landscape painters in their sixties admitted to a newspaper that they had flattened the overnight crop circles in southern England with a wooden plank and a rope. Why did they keep the joke going for over a decade, and why did they speak up?
For anyone who has seen aerial photos of crop circles and heard the alien theories, but has never heard this 1991 story.

The third file from Curiosity Case Files. The popular stories: UFO landing marks, charged whirlwinds, and shapes no human could make. The recorded account: an idea in a pub in the late 1970s (reports give 1976 or 1978), inspired by Australia's 1966 "saucer nest"; a plank, rope, and a wire loop on a baseball cap; a circle made in Kent in 1991 with a reporter watching, which an invited researcher declared no human could have made. The circles continued after the confession: new makers openly took commissions, and the patterns grew more complex. We end with three questions about the claim that a pattern near Stonehenge appeared in "45 minutes" in 1996, then examine farmers' losses and the law: flattening crops in someone else's field is criminal damage.

We cover admissions, demonstrations, and documented events, and state where sources disagree. Information current to 2026-10-10.

Illustrations are AI-generated. Recent real people appear only from behind or in distant views. Photos are public-domain archival images; see the image credits for their sources.

g48i.text: In 1991, TIME also covered crop circles.

ji6j.text: Field oddities had inspired stories before.

abr4.text: A 1678 British pamphlet said a devil cut all the oats overnight.

5p7h.text: Called the earliest record, it shows cutting, not pressing.

52pf.text: Who made the first crop circle, and when?

mgp6.text: The answer lay in a pub. Two old friends had a drink every Friday.

c9is.text: One was Doug, one Dave. Both were landscape painters.

jkpy.text: Both lived in Hampshire; Doug ran a frame shop.

zbdi.text: Doug moved to Australia, returning to Britain years later.

2wsg.text: He had read an odd story in an Australian newspaper.

f9m4.text: In 1966, a Queensland farmer said he saw a flying saucer take off.

rqm4.text: A circle remained in the reeds, called a saucer nest.

nffc.text: Doug told Dave. They wanted it to look like a saucer had landed.

97u4.text: It was the late 1970s. Some reports say 1976; others, 1978.

u4nc.text: According to makers' accounts, they first used an iron bar.

u8zr.text: That iron bar originally secured the frame shop's back door.

7mey.text: The first was one simple circle, about 9 metres across.

4cqc.text: To be clear: it was someone else's field and crops they damaged.

xm5r.text: Later, Doug stood at the centre and held the rope.

n9pn.text: Dave held a wood plank flat at knee height.

nnct.text: He walked around the centre, pushing wheat over with it.

zc29.text: A wire loop through a baseball cap's brim served as a sight.

sk9s.text: Their tools: a wooden plank, a ball of string, and a baseball cap.

35mn.text: But nobody noticed their circles for the first 3 years.

r3hc.text: Doug said his wife first noticed the car's high mileage.

9eku.text: He showed his press scrapbook, took her to a field; she believed him.

7kew.text: Around 1980, a newspaper finally reported it.

q4u7.text: A later obituary quoted the report's headline:

jq58.text: How did their joke become a nationwide mystery?

fg56.text: A meteorologist said an atmospheric phenomenon made the circles.

prze.text: Rotating air columns picked up charged matter and flattened crops below.

h763.text: He named his theory the plasma vortex.

3njc.text: A retired engineer co-wrote a book that sold over 50,000 copies.

2pze.text: Both wanted to show the circles weren't weather-related.

9h95.text: They turned one circle into groups of several.

yru3.text: Later, straight lines began appearing in the patterns.

kqrd.text: The meteorologist admitted straight-line designs were man-made.

xxc9.text: But he stressed simple circles could still be atmospheric.

ga8k.text: Crop circles were either hoaxes or caused by air vortices.

dq9t.text: How many did they make? Britannica says over 200.

7mp5.text: TIME wrote of up to 20 or 30 new circles each season.

a755.text: They weren't alone. Copycats had already appeared.

wx2j.text: Fans even sought government research funding.

i3qu.text: With the joke so big, why did they speak up?

xxwq.text: September 1991. There are two accounts of why they spoke up.

dj8u.text: TIME said it was because fans sought government funding.

zeib.text: An obituary years later said going public was Dave's idea.

rh83.text: That year, Doug was 67 and Dave was 62.

v6zv.text: The British tabloid Today first broke the story.

2r37.text: In Kent, they made a circle with a reporter watching.

vyy3.text: The reporter invited the book's author to see it.

9a4t.text: No human could have done this.

48iv.text: Doug replied: I'm afraid we've been having you on.

vnvf.text: The researcher said: We've all been conned.

gffu.text: The verdict: genuine, beyond human ability.

s5u9.text: In fact, two elderly men made it, with the reporter watching throughout.

vrcc.text: September 9's headline: Men Who Conned the World.

jfde.text: Later, they did it again for reporters in a Hampshire field.

xpcc.text: Another researcher said nothing here impressed him.

d5z5.text: He later said: They made some, but the phenomenon remains.

5xuj.text: He asked: Canada has circles too. Did they take a plank?

zf53.text: The next year, they won the Ig Nobel Prize in Physics.

mdex.text: The mystery was revealed. Why didn't crop circles stop?

ffic.text: Because they were already not the only makers.

ncp6.text: By summer 1991, others were already making them in fields.

dauc.text: Some designs already went beyond what the two men could make.

h9vk.text: Their patterns inspired a second wave of makers.

px5z.text: Art groups openly took commissions to make circles for ads.

vxj4.text: Their clients included cereal brands, telecom companies, and TV shows.

zkst.text: Makers said a newspaper commission paid a farmer £6,000.

ytin.text: The damaged crops were worth only about £100.

xeb8.text: Designs grew more complex, with up to 2,000 separate shapes.

vz6a.text: In 1998, a TV crew filmed a team making 100 circles.

kxv8.text: They flattened roughly one circle per minute.

ccht.text: Here's the aerial view. This photo is from Switzerland in 2007.

58ph.text: It was far more than one circle.

p2sw.text: A famous one appeared near Stonehenge in July 1996.

fq9d.text: The story goes: at 5:30 p.m., a doctor flew over in a small plane.

dmiu.text: It wasn't there. Flying back 45 minutes later, he saw it.

57u4.text: So some said no human could have made it that fast.

6cv6.text: Who made that claim? A maker said three people did it the night before.

4c7d.text: What remains unclear? Each side has just one person's account.

46n4.text: The maker said it took 2 hours 45 minutes; the doctor simply missed it.

upfz.text: He didn't claim he made it. The interview wasn't recorded.

hx29.text: That same month, another design had 194 circles.

ijkv.text: A researcher said electromagnetic rays lengthened wheat stem nodes.

wtat.text: Critics said his statistics and sampling were flawed.

ikcn.text: They said flattened wheat naturally grows differently.

zir6.text: A physicist said those studies were neither confirmed nor disproved.

2uwr.text: After all that, whose wheat field was it?

87cp.text: Beneath every circle lies a farmer's harvest.

bih4.text: In 2017, a 60-metre-wide circle flattened 2 acres of wheat.

eirw.text: The farmer put a bucket in the field for visitor donations.

32xp.text: At another farm in 2010, visitors were asked to leave £5 to enter.

sdxu.text: The Guardian counted 92 circles from 2018 to 2022.

vsgd.text: Tourism was the other side. In 2004, a worker at the Avebury visitor center said:

md6j.text: 80 to 90 per cent of summer trade was tied to crop circles.

avsx.text: The law is clear: Wiltshire police call it criminal damage.

vj4x.text: In 2000, a man pleaded guilty and was fined £100.

ukvc.text: A farmers' union member: It's like wrecking your garden.

tiie.text: So the story about that plank is a record, not an invitation.

u597.text: Late in life, he said he regretted telling everyone.

m657.text: A maker imagined him saying: It's only flattened wheat.

sr6f.text: To me, who made them isn't the most interesting part.

9wn4.text: It's why people still did not believe it after the answer came out.

pa32.text: Don't mock believers. The two men called it a joke.
